title: Lecture 05 - Distributed systems: load balancer design, remote and distributed locks

questions.q: What four agenda items were written on the board for this class, in order?
questions.answer: Approaching distributed systems; designing a load balancer; remote and distributed locks; synchronizing consumers.

questions.q: Why did the teacher call the load balancer the core component that makes distributed systems possible?
questions.answer: Because it abstracts away the details of having multiple servers in the backend: clients see one endpoint.

questions.q: How many lines of core code did the teacher say a basic load balancer needs?
questions.answer: Hardly about 10 lines of core logic (and he said even that was an exaggeration); the copy part is about two lines.

questions.q: Why are remote and distributed locks called the heart of data correctness in distributed systems?
questions.answer: Multiple processes on different machines must coordinate so data stays consistent, e.g. two distributed transactions trying to update the same row: one must stop the other, and there is no single database to do it.

questions.q: What is a distributed system, as defined in class and on the board?
questions.answer: Multiple components on multiple machines that appear to an outsider (end user, another microservice, an internal portal) as a single coherent system that solves a bigger problem; the distributedness is abstracted away.

questions.q: What did the teacher's professor say is both the best and the worst thing about distributed systems, and what design rule follows?
questions.answer: Anything that could go wrong would go wrong (Murphy's law). So assume everything and anything can fail and check that your system still handles it; otherwise you cannot guarantee correctness (e.g. a broken distributed transaction leaves corrupt data).

questions.q: What is a day zero architecture?
questions.answer: Don't over-complicate on day zero: one machine, one server, one database, one cache. Then scale each component independently.

questions.q: List the steps of the design loop on the board in order, and say what the arrow does.
questions.answer: Start with a Day0 architecture and scale each component; see how it performs under load; rectify the system; re-architect; and repeat. A curved arrow goes from the bottom of the list back to the top: it is a loop.

questions.q: When you see how the system performs under load, what level of detail did the teacher say matters?
questions.answer: The low-level details (what happens at the code level when the service runs) are the pain points, not only the high-level picture; he compared it to zooming in with a microscope again and again.

questions.q: What three reasons for distributed systems were written under 'Why distributed systems?'
questions.answer: Scale, horizontal scalability, fault tolerance.

questions.q: A team has API servers behind an auto-scaling policy and calls its system distributed and horizontally scalable. What did the teacher say is wrong with that claim?
questions.answer: Having more machines or auto-scaling API servers is not enough. Every layer (database, cache, stateful and stateless services, API servers, load balancer, CDN) must be checked for horizontal scalability; any layer that is not becomes a single point of failure.

questions.q: What must you know about your service to claim real horizontal scalability, and what goes wrong if you don't?
questions.answer: Its unit economics: how much load (requests, processing) one server can handle, so you can scale linearly (linear amplification). Without it you just add machines blindly and leak money by under- or over-provisioning.

questions.q: Is it acceptable to keep a database that is not horizontally scalable?
questions.answer: Yes, cutting that corner is fine so long as it can handle the load.

questions.q: Why did Flipkart have to build its own load balancer?
questions.answer: It runs private, on-premise infrastructure (its own data centres), so it can't just use a cloud load balancer.

questions.q: What two advantages of using a load balancer were written on the board?
questions.answer: Fault tolerance and no over-clocked (overloaded) server.

questions.q: Describe the first load balancer diagram on the board.
questions.answer: Two users on the left, each with a line to one Load Balancer box in the middle, which has lines to three API boxes on the right.

questions.q: Why does a client not need to know the backend servers?
questions.answer: The load balancer is a single point of entry with one domain name or IP that does not change; clients talk only to it and it forwards each request to one of the backend servers.

questions.q: How does round robin work, and how common is it?
questions.answer: It is the default algorithm on almost all load balancers. The LB remembers which backend got the last request and sends the next one to the next server: 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3...

questions.q: When should you use round robin?
questions.answer: With uniform infrastructure (same machine configuration) and a uniform load pattern: every API responds in a narrow time range (e.g. under one second), so response time has low variance and it doesn't matter which server gets a request.

questions.q: In the round-robin diagram, which request numbers did each of the three backends get?
questions.answer: Top 1,4; middle 2,5; bottom 3,6.

questions.q: In the weighted round robin example (4 GB, 8 GB, 4 GB machines), what goes wrong with plain round robin and what ratio fixes it?
questions.answer: Each gets the same share, so if the 4 GB machines run at 80% the 8 GB machine (twice the cores) runs at about 40%: under-utilised. Weighted round robin sends requests in the ratio 1:2:1.

questions.q: In the weighted round robin diagram, how is the bigger machine drawn and what do the request numbers show?
questions.answer: The middle backend is drawn wider with a yellow outline (bigger machine) and receives more requests (2,3,6,...) than the others (top 1,5; bottom 4,8).

questions.q: What real situation made the teacher use weighted round robin?
questions.answer: His team bought AWS reserved instances of different sizes by mistake and AWS would not change them; rather than keep them idle they put them into existing workloads behind weighted round robin.

questions.q: Where do you configure the balancing algorithm, and what if your cloud does not show the option?
questions.answer: Every load balancer offers a set of algorithms with their own config; read its official docs. If the option is missing (it may be behind a feature flag), raise a support ticket with the cloud provider.

questions.q: What recurring theme did the teacher draw from the algorithm choice?
questions.answer: It is always about money: are you utilising your infrastructure well? Saving money for the organisation is a quantified impact (and easy to pitch for promotion).

questions.q: How does least connections choose a backend?
questions.answer: The LB tracks how many active connections it has to each backend and sends a new request to the one with the fewest.

questions.q: Why is the number of open connections a reasonable measure of how busy a backend is?
questions.answer: Without connection pooling, a connection stays open only while the server is working on the request (it closes when the response is sent), so more open connections means a busier server; sending to the least-connected one improves the chance of a quick response.

questions.q: When should you use least connections? Give the class example.
questions.answer: When response times have a big variance, e.g. analytics: some queries answer in one second, some in an hour or two.

questions.q: Why does plain round robin perform badly for such high-variance workloads?
questions.answer: It ignores how busy a server is, so long-running requests can keep landing on a server that is already busy with long-running work, bogging it down; least connections sends to a relatively free machine.

questions.q: Why shouldn't the load balancer pick backends using their CPU and memory usage?
questions.answer: It would need to call another system, query and analyse usage, adding network calls and multiple milliseconds of latency; the LB must decide in microseconds. So it uses a heuristic it already has: its own connection counts. It stays simple and stateless.

questions.q: In the least-connections diagram, which request numbers did each backend get?
questions.answer: Top 1,5,7; middle 2,4,8,9; bottom 3,6,10.

questions.q: Must a least-connections load balancer keep persistent connections to all backends?
questions.answer: No. It can be fully stateless, or keep a connection pool; with a pool it must count least active connections (e.g. a pool of 100 with 2 in use means 2 active).

questions.q: How can a request take an hour if HTTP closes the connection after the response?
questions.answer: Think raw TCP: a TCP connection stays open until the network, the client or the server breaks it. HTTP keep-alive keeps it open too, and gRPC over HTTP/2 does not terminate unless someone explicitly closes it.

questions.q: A student worried that least connections may send to a server whose long query is about to finish. What was the answer?
questions.answer: Local optimisation is good enough, no need for global optimisation; with such workloads you'd have many servers, not three. Data warehouses (BigQuery, Redshift) use least-connection balancing across clusters for exactly this mix of short and long queries.

questions.q: If a user closes the browser during a long request and resubmits, does the work run twice, and can it be stopped?
questions.answer: It's business logic: once TCP breaks it's broken, and a submitted job keeps running; long jobs should be asynchronous. You can implement cancelling (the socket tells you the connection closed), as Redshift and BigQuery do, but normal HTTP web servers don't give you the tooling.

questions.q: What three requirements for the load balancer design were written on the board?
questions.answer: Balance the load; tunable algorithm; scaling beyond one machine.

questions.q: When the teacher benchmarked his own Go load balancer against Nginx and HAProxy, what did he find and conclude?
questions.answer: His was 5-6x faster, but only because Nginx and HAProxy do much more than his simple load balancer.

questions.q: What is the difference between an LB server and a backend server?
questions.answer: The LB server is the machine running the load balancer process (what we are building). Backend servers are the services requests are forwarded to (payments, auth, profile), treated as black boxes.

questions.q: What kind of process is the load balancer, and what IP does the single LB server have in the example?
questions.answer: A normal TCP server process (not even HTTP) on a VM, with a static IP 10.0.0.1 that does not change.

questions.q: In the single-LB diagram, what addresses and ports did the LB server and the backends have, and what does the LB store?
questions.answer: LB server 10.0.0.1, listening on port 9000. Backends 10.0.0.7, 10.0.0.8, 10.0.0.9, each serving on port 8081. Under the LB is its in-memory list B.Servs: [10.0.0.7:8081, 10.0.0.8:8081, 10.0.0.9:8081].

questions.q: What two things do you need to connect to any server?
questions.answer: Its IP address and port number.

questions.q: How many TCP connections exist for one client request through the load balancer, and between whom?
questions.answer: Two: one between client and LB server, one between LB server and the chosen backend server.

questions.q: What mapping does the LB server keep, and where?
questions.answer: Which source TCP connection (client-LB) maps to which target TCP connection (LB-backend), in an in-memory hash table; you cannot store a TCP connection in a database.

questions.q: Does the load balancer need to understand HTTP?
questions.answer: No. It reads bytes from one socket and writes them to the other; the packets could be HTTP, WebSocket, RTMP or anything.

questions.q: Trace the response path back to the client in the two-connection diagram.
questions.answer: The backend writes the response on TCP2 (the connection it received from); the LB sees data from TCP2, looks up the map (TCP2 to TCP1) and writes it to TCP1, so the client gets it.

questions.q: With a second client, what does the LB's connection map look like on the board?
questions.answer: { tcp1 -> tcp2, tcp3 -> tcp4 }: user 2 connects on TCP3 and the LB opens TCP4 to the bottom backend.

questions.q: What does the two-connections-per-request design imply for one LB server?
questions.answer: It must manage 2x as many TCP connections as clients, so one LB server isn't enough: you need multiple LB servers and must scale horizontally.

questions.q: How can you build and test a load balancer on a single machine?
questions.answer: Run the LB process on a port like 9000 and three backend processes on different ports (8081, 8082, 8083) on localhost, since only one process can listen on a port; no cloud, VMs or Docker needed.

questions.q: In the code walkthrough, which port did the LB listen on and how were the backends set up?
questions.answer: The LB listened on port 9090. Four backends were hard-coded: Flask hello-world processes on localhost ports 8081-8084, spun from the same code base.

questions.q: What does the LB's accept loop do when a client connects?
questions.answer: An infinite for loop waits on listener.Accept(); the accepted TCP connection is wrapped as the source connection with a request ID and handed to proxy() in its own goroutine.

questions.q: What are the steps inside proxy()?
questions.answer: Get a backend from the strategy (lb.strategy.GetNextBackend), dial a TCP connection to its host:port (sending 'backend not available' if that fails), increment NumRequests, then run io.Copy(backendConn, srcConn) and io.Copy(srcConn, backendConn).

questions.q: Why do the two io.Copy calls run in their own goroutines?
questions.answer: io.Copy is a blocking call that keeps copying until it receives EOF (the connection terminates); run inline it would block, so request copying and response copying each run in their own goroutine in parallel.

questions.q: How is round robin implemented in strategy.go?
questions.answer: GetNextBackend does Index = (Index + 1) % len(Backends) and returns Backends[Index].

questions.q: Which balancing strategies did the teacher's code implement?
questions.answer: Round robin, static, and hashed (consistent hashing).

questions.q: Did the demo load balancer track connection counts, and how would you know a connection ended?
questions.answer: No. It only tracked NumRequests per backend (to check round robin works). A terminated connection raises a panic/exception you can catch to update in-memory state.

questions.q: Is the LB-to-backend communication a REST call?
questions.answer: No, it is a raw TCP connection; whatever arrives on one side is copied to the other (HTTP, RPC, any packet).

questions.q: What is the difference between building and scaling, according to the teacher?
questions.answer: Anyone can build systems (load balancer, CDN, Docker started locally) on one machine; scaling needs multiple machines and few get to do it. Build things locally to learn the low-level details.

questions.q: If an LB server has a 10,000 TCP connection limit, how many concurrent clients can it serve and why?
questions.answer: 5,000, because every client connection needs a second connection to a backend.

questions.q: What four factors did the class brainstorm for the load balancer design?
questions.answer: LB configurations, monitoring, availability, extensibility.

questions.q: What is the bare minimum configuration a load balancer must store (as written on the board)?
questions.answer: The backend servers (ip:port of each) and the balancing algorithm; later the health_endpoint was added.

questions.q: Why shouldn't the LB server read its configuration from the database on every request?
questions.answer: Each network call costs about 3-5 ms, and the LB already adds a network hop, so it would slow every request.

questions.q: What is the fix for that, and what new problem does it create?
questions.answer: Load the config from the DB when the LB server starts and keep an in-memory copy. The problem: keeping that copy in sync when the config changes, e.g. a backend server goes down.

questions.q: What component detects that a backend server went down?
questions.answer: An orchestrator, which runs health checks (heartbeats) against the backend servers.

questions.q: Why check a health endpoint instead of just checking that the backend VM is up?
questions.answer: The VM can be up while the service process has crashed (e.g. divide-by-zero or null pointer exception); what matters is that the service is up, not the server.

questions.q: What does the health check endpoint look like and how is it used?
questions.answer: Each backend's web server exposes an endpoint like /status or /health on its service port (8081). It is part of the LB configuration (health_endpoint); the orchestrator calls it continuously and expects a 200 response.

questions.q: In the brainstorm diagram, which way do the heartbeat arrows point, and where does the orchestrator write?
questions.answer: The hb arrows go from the orchestrator to each backend (B Srv1-3); a line goes from the orchestrator into the DB. B Srv2 is hatched (down).

questions.q: What does the orchestrator do when backend server 2 fails its health check?
questions.answer: It removes (marks dead) backend server 2's entry in the database.

questions.q: Why is having the LB servers poll the database for config changes a bad idea? Use the class numbers.
questions.answer: Polling has a frequency, e.g. every 10 s. If a backend dies just after a poll, for up to N-1 seconds (about 9 s) the LB keeps sending requests from its stale in-memory copy to the dead server, causing an error-rate spike for users.

questions.q: A student said LB polling hurts because health checking adds latency to user requests. What did the teacher correct?
questions.answer: The orchestrator does the health checks, not the LB server, so user requests aren't affected by them; the real problem with polling is staleness between polls.

questions.q: What were the two sources of configuration changes in the design?
questions.answer: Health check results written by the orchestrator, and developers changing config through the LB console/APIs (e.g. adding backends in the AWS console, changing the algorithm or health check).

questions.q: What was the first push-based approach (the student's)?
questions.answer: Run a second process on the LB server on another port (9091, a meta/admin port next to the 9090 data port); whoever changes the config calls it, and its handler re-reads the config from the DB and updates the in-memory copy. Near-immediate.

questions.q: What was the teacher's reactive approach for pushing config changes?
questions.answer: A real-time Pub/Sub broker such as Redis: when the DB config changes, an event is published (by CDC on the DB, or by the orchestrator or LB console); every LB server is subscribed and updates its in-memory copy.

questions.q: In the diagram, how did the CDC path replace the periodic sync?
questions.answer: The dotted 'syn-' curve from the LB to the DB was removed; instead a CDC line goes from the DB into a pipe (broker) and from the pipe up into the LB.

questions.q: Which of the two push approaches is right?
questions.answer: Both. There's no one right answer; it's a trade-off and each fits some situations. The key idea: polling doesn't work, make it reactive.

questions.q: Which earlier system design did the teacher reuse the real-time Pub/Sub idea from?
questions.answer: Slack's real-time communication (last session), where polling was also rejected in favour of immediate push.

questions.q: Besides health, what must the orchestrator watch on the LB servers, and why?
questions.answer: Whether they are overwhelmed: CPU, memory, network and disk vitals, so it can add an LB server when load is high and remove one when it drops (LB servers must scale horizontally too).

questions.q: Why not just have the orchestrator call each LB server for its current CPU?
questions.answer: You need historical data and trends, not one instant: if you only look when it's at 100% you have no time to react; you want to act at 60-80% and know averages. It needs a generic approach.

questions.q: What kind of data are the vitals, compared with the LB config?
questions.answer: Time-series data (CPU, memory, disk, network over time), whereas the config is key-value.

questions.q: A student proposed the orchestrator keep its own database fed by LB heartbeat messages carrying CPU. What was the teacher's response?
questions.answer: Don't re-implement what other systems already do; reuse existing tools.

questions.q: Where should the vitals go and who sends them?
questions.answer: Telemetry agents on every VM (LB servers and backend servers) push metrics to a central store like Prometheus; the orchestrator periodically queries it for average utilisation to scale LB or backend servers.

questions.q: How does an autoscaling group work, according to the teacher?
questions.answer: You configure a policy like 'if average CPU utilisation is X, do Y'; internally it queries a metrics store and takes action when the condition is met.

questions.q: In the brainstorm diagram, how was the metrics store connected?
questions.answer: A cylinder 'Metric Vitals' labelled Prometheus (monitoring) at top right: a line from the LB servers' agents into it, and green curves connecting it to B Srv1-3 and to the orchestrator.

questions.q: Why can't the LB servers share one IP address, and what abstracts multiple IPs?
questions.answer: An IP address is fixed to a machine, so two machines can't serve the same IP, which would stop LB servers from scaling. A domain name abstracts multiple IP addresses.

questions.q: A student said putting LBs in DNS makes them public. What misconception did the teacher correct?
questions.answer: That DNS means public DNS. Many load balancers (e.g. for internal microservices) are private, and DNS can be private: you run your own DNS server inside your infrastructure.

questions.q: What DNS server did the teacher recommend for private infrastructure, and how do machines use it?
questions.answer: CoreDNS (used across the Kubernetes world), a lightweight DNS server; each machine is configured with it as its DNS address so domain names resolve through it.

questions.q: When a domain name maps to several LB IPs, how does DNS pick one?
questions.answer: Using the same strategies: round robin, weighted round robin, etc.

questions.q: Does the DNS server route requests to the load balancer?
questions.answer: No. DNS is not a proxy (that would make it the load balancer and a bottleneck). It only resolves the name to an IP and returns it; the client caches it for some time and connects to the LB server directly.

questions.q: What does the DNS part of the brainstorm diagram show?
questions.answer: CoreDNS / DNS box mapping payments.lb.google.com to 10.0.0.1, 10.0.0.2 (later 10.0.0.3); arrows between the user and DNS (lookup and answer), then user to LB; a line from DNS to the orchestrator.

questions.q: How does a new LB server become reachable?
questions.answer: The orchestrator spins it up and adds its IP to the DNS entry for the load balancer's domain.

questions.q: Trace a request through the final load balancer design.
questions.answer: Client looks up lb.payments.google.com in CoreDNS, gets an LB server IP (e.g. 10.0.0.1), connects to that LB server; it picks a backend via its balancing strategy; the backend processes and the response goes back through the LB to the client.

questions.q: Trace a configuration change through the final design.
questions.answer: A change (health check failure, autoscaling, developer via LB console) updates the DB; CDC (or the orchestrator/LB console) publishes to Redis Pub/Sub; it is broadcast in real time to all LB servers, which update their in-memory config copy.

questions.q: What were the orchestrator's focused responsibilities on the prepared page?
questions.answer: Keep an eye on the health of backend servers; if one is unhealthy, update the DB ({b_servers: [...]}), and the change reaches LB servers through Pub/Sub; monitor health of LB servers and scale them up and down. (Plus: read about the phi-accrual failure detection algorithm.)

questions.q: On what will the orchestrator scale LB servers, and where does that data come from?
questions.answer: CPU, memory and number of TCP connections; from the monitoring component, Prometheus (the orchestrator queries it).

questions.q: In the final design, what label sits above the orchestrator and what feeds the Autoscaling box?
questions.answer: 'leaderElec' (leader election) above the orchestrator; Autoscaling gets a line from Prometheus and points into the LB Console.

questions.q: Which paper did the teacher recommend for load balancers?
questions.answer: Maglev: A Fast and Reliable Software Load Balancer (Google).

questions.q: A client's local DNS cache still holds the IP of an LB server that died. Must it wait for the TTL?
questions.answer: No: when connecting fails, the client reacts immediately, invalidates its cache and asks CoreDNS for another IP.

questions.q: What if CoreDNS itself goes down, and how do you find a working CoreDNS?
questions.answer: Run multiple CoreDNS servers, with a DNS for CoreDNS. At the end there is one tiny single point of failure with a standby node, the base condition of the recursion; it is very unlikely to fail and the standby takes over.

questions.q: External end users use public DNS from their OS, not your CoreDNS. How do they reach the load balancer?
questions.answer: Then the LB is public and resolved through public DNS (e.g. Route 53), so the private CoreDNS isn't in the path; in practice intermediate proxy layers sit between (read Maglev).

questions.q: Does each LB server balance traffic for every service?
questions.answer: No. A load balancer balances across a homogeneous set of servers (it is not an API gateway); each service has its own load balancer / LB servers with its own CoreDNS entries.

questions.q: What is a lock manager?
questions.answer: A remote machine that tracks which item is locked by which machine so the machines can coordinate (locks managed by a central machine).

questions.q: How did locking in the airline check-in system differ from what distributed systems need?
questions.answer: There the lock was in the database's memory, one machine/one process, so it was just memory updates. With multiple machines that must coordinate you need a remote lock manager.

questions.q: How do multiple threads synchronize, and why?
questions.answer: Through in-memory constructs (mutex, semaphore, explicit locks, atomic instructions), because RAM is what threads share.

questions.q: Explain the apt-get example.
questions.answer: Running apt-get upgrade in two terminals fails: the first process creates a dpkg lock file; a second instance sees the file exists and exits; when the first finishes it deletes the file. Processes share the disk, so they synchronize through it.

questions.q: Complete the three board lines on synchronization, and state the general principle.
questions.answer: Multiple threads synchronize through mutex & semaphore; multiple processes through disk; multiple machines through a remote lock. Use the closest storage that is shared: RAM, then disk, then network.

questions.q: Describe the hypothetical queue used to motivate remote locks and what we want.
questions.answer: A remote queue with zero protection: queue.pop isn't thread safe, so concurrent consumers may get the same message. It is a black box we can't change. We want only one of three consumers to read from it at any time.

questions.q: Why were the proposals 'a synchronized block', 'a lock on the queue's server' and 'a layer in front of the queue' rejected?
questions.answer: The queue is remote, so a local synchronized block doesn't help; the queue and its server are a black box you can't change or access; adding a layer is not the lock manager the problem asks for.

questions.q: How does a database act as the lock manager for queue 7?
questions.answer: Store a key Q7 whose value is the consumer that owns the lock (e.g. consumer 1). Only that consumer reads; others see someone else's name and wait. When done it removes its name, and the others compete to write theirs.

questions.q: What does a lock manager fundamentally need to store?
questions.answer: The resource and who owns it.

questions.q: What happens if a consumer dies while holding the lock, and the fix?
questions.answer: It never deletes its entry, so the lock is held perpetually. Every lock entry needs a TTL (automatic expiration) so it deletes itself.

questions.q: Which three properties must the lock store provide, and which database gives all of them?
questions.answer: Key-value access, atomic instructions and TTL (k,v / Atomic / TTL on the board). Redis gives all three, hence Redis-based Redlock.

questions.q: Give the consumer's pseudocode in order.
questions.answer: ACQ_LOCK(), READ_MSG(), REL_LOCK(). All consumers wait on ACQ_LOCK while one of them reads the message.

questions.q: What two requirements from the lock manager did the board list, and why each?
questions.answer: Atomic operations, so that two machines do not both ACQ_LOCK; automatic expiration, to avoid perpetual locking.

questions.q: Which databases did the board list for this, and why is Redis popular?
questions.answer: Redis and DynamoDB; Redis is the popular choice because it is in-memory (fast).

questions.q: What does the example lock entry 'queue7 : consumer 2 [ex : 300]' mean?
questions.answer: The lock on queue7 is held by consumer 2, expiring after 300 s (5 minutes).

questions.q: Write the logic of acquire_lock.
questions.answer: consumer_id = get_my_id(); while True: v = redis.setnx(q, consumer_id, ex=300); if v == 1 return (you own the lock, go read); else continue (spin).

questions.q: Why use SETNX, and what makes it safe with many consumers?
questions.answer: SETNX sets the key only if it doesn't exist (returns 1 if set, 0 if not), so it won't overwrite an existing owner. Each Redis command is atomic: while it runs no other command executes, so only one concurrent attempt succeeds.

questions.q: What goes wrong if release_lock simply deletes the key?
questions.answer: A process can delete a lock it doesn't own. Timeout case: C1's 5-minute TTL expires mid-processing, Redis deletes the key, C2 acquires the lock, then C1 finishes and deletes C2's lock.

questions.q: Release with 'get owner; if it is me, delete' still has an edge case. What is it?
questions.answer: Between the get and the delete the key can expire and C2 can acquire it, so C1's check passed but it deletes C2's lock.

questions.q: How is that release race fixed?
questions.answer: Run the get-compare-delete as one Lua script through Redis EVAL: Redis executes the whole script atomically, so nobody can acquire the lock in between.

questions.q: What habit did the teacher recommend for reasoning about distributed code like this?
questions.answer: Imagine that after every single line something lags or goes down, and check the system still works correctly.

questions.q: What is wrong with a single Redis instance as lock manager?
questions.answer: It's not fault tolerant: a single point of failure. If it goes down no one can acquire the lock and the whole system stalls.

questions.q: Why do distributed locks exist, and who needs them?
questions.answer: Only to remove the single point of failure of a single lock instance. Most startups never use them because cloud services give the guarantees; companies building those (AWS, GCP, Google's Chubby) do.

questions.q: How is the Redlock setup arranged?
questions.answer: Five Redis master nodes, all independent: no replication, no multi-master.

questions.q: Give the Redlock acquire steps from the board.
questions.answer: Client goes through the 5 nodes trying ACQ_LOCK (with timeout); if acquired on > 50% (3 of 5) then ACQUIRED; else release the lock on the instances acquired and return FAILED.

questions.q: What is the cost of distributed locking and where should it be used?
questions.answer: It hurts performance; throughput goes for a toss. So not in high-throughput systems; use it where a high degree of correctness and fault tolerance is required.

questions.q: Is Redlock fully correct?
questions.answer: No. Edge cases remain (e.g. nodes holding your locks going down), but it reduces the probability to a bare minimum; tolerating one node down is fine.

questions.q: What did the board answer to 'But why are we doing this?'
questions.answer: With distributed locking we now do not have a SPoF.

questions.q: What further reading on locks did the teacher give?
questions.answer: Google's Chubby paper (lock service for loosely coupled distributed systems), Martin Kleppmann's blog on why not to use Redlock (a rare edge case), plus his blogs and YouTube videos on distributed transactions.

questions.q: Here we distributed the lock store. Was that for scale?
questions.answer: No, it reduces throughput. It gives fault tolerance, reliability and availability. Pick your pattern: scale horizontally to handle load, or make it distributed for fault tolerance.

questions.q: A student proposed a network-level lock: a server that accepts only one connection at a time. What did the teacher think?
questions.answer: A brilliant idea: a TCP server that accepts one client and doesn't accept another until it's done; if the consumer dies its connection drops. Easy to implement in a few hours.

questions.q: Can MySQL be used instead of Redis for the lock?
questions.answer: Yes, if you handle TTL yourself, e.g. a cron job removing expired locks; otherwise you get perpetual locks. Focus on core properties, not the database.

questions.q: Is the Lua language itself what makes the release atomic?
questions.answer: No. Redis supports executing Lua scripts inside the Redis server via EVAL; you pass the script from Python instead of separate commands and Redis runs it atomically.

questions.q: Real queues (SQS, RabbitMQ, Kafka, OCI's visibility setting) already stop two consumers getting a message. Why the lock?
questions.answer: The queue was hypothetical, with zero protection, chosen to understand remote locks; real queues give these guarantees so you don't need to.

questions.q: What stops a consumer from reading the queue without taking the lock?
questions.answer: Nothing in the queue; it's our consumer code, and we write it to acquire the lock first, then read.

questions.q: How does MongoDB use remote locks?
questions.answer: A distributed transaction updating documents on shards 1, 3 and 5 takes locks on them, tracked by its own lock manager; another transaction wanting the same documents waits until the first commits or rolls back.

questions.q: What is the only thing shared between multiple machines for synchronization?
questions.answer: The network: neither RAM nor disk. Even two clusters synchronize over the network.

questions.q: Doesn't the TTL cap how long a process may hold a lock?
questions.answer: Yes, every implementation has it; without it you run a bigger risk: perpetual locking that stalls the whole system.

questions.q: Which is costlier: mutex signalling or a network lock?
questions.answer: The network lock. A mutex is in-memory and trivial for the OS (two lines in C); the network is the costliest mode of communication.

questions.q: If everything runs on a single server, what should you use instead of Redis?
questions.answer: A normal mutex / synchronized / atomic instructions around the critical section; no Redis needed.

questions.q: In Redlock, if a client holds 3 locks and two of those nodes go down, can two clients hold the lock? How is it minimized?
questions.answer: Yes, that is the edge case. It's minimized: clients without a majority keep releasing their locks, and the majority holder keeps trying to acquire the remaining nodes (within a few seconds); you could also wait for an unhealthy cluster to recover. Never fully mitigated, only minimized.

questions.q: Why should a client that already holds the majority keep acquiring locks on the remaining nodes?
questions.answer: To minimize that edge case: if it holds locks on all nodes, losing two nodes still leaves it the majority.

questions.q: How did the teacher test Redlock edge cases without many machines?
questions.answer: Five Redis processes on his laptop (ports 6379-6383), with injected delays of 1, 5 and 15 seconds and heavy load.

questions.q: Why not just use ZooKeeper instead of Redis-based locking?
questions.answer: ZooKeeper does essentially the same thing; you may use it. Its notification framework is a real-time Pub/Sub over persistent TCP connections, so it could replace Redis Pub/Sub in the LB design too. Engineers should know how it works inside.

questions.q: Why do many young organisations pick Redis over ZooKeeper?
questions.answer: They're intimidated by ZooKeeper and associate it with Java; Redis is familiar and lets them build a scrappy solution. Choose by core properties and stack comfort.

questions.q: Can a consumer read multiple messages from a queue at once?
questions.answer: It depends on the queue's guarantees; SQS lets you read up to 10 messages per call.

questions.q: Does DNS send traffic to a second load balancer when the first is heavily loaded?
questions.answer: No. DNS only maps a domain to several IPs and round-robins between them; it has no load information.

questions.q: How do you run active-passive load balancers behind DNS?
questions.answer: Keep only the active LB's IP in DNS, or weighted round robin with weight 0 for the passive one; the orchestrator updates DNS on failover. DNS is a dumb hash map.

questions.q: For sticky sessions, do you need a separate session service?
questions.answer: No. Use consistent hashing in the LB (a plain array in its memory); a separate service adds a network hop.

questions.q: What did the teacher say about adding services to a design?
questions.answer: Every service is a network hop adding 3-10 ms of latency; don't add boxes without justification (a good architecture he saw had four microservices handling petabytes).

questions.q: Does round robin require session state?
questions.answer: No, it only keeps an integer index into the backend array.

questions.q: Is CoreDNS's choice of LB IP a bottleneck that undoes the LB algorithm?
questions.answer: No. CoreDNS just picks an IP (round robin/random); the balancing algorithm runs on the LB servers.

questions.q: Why have separate heartbeats if Prometheus already has metrics?
questions.answer: Prometheus is for vitals; a generic vitals-ingestion system usually doesn't do health checks, so heartbeats stay explicit.

questions.q: Why Redis Pub/Sub rather than server-sent events?
questions.answer: The need is real-time broadcast to all LB servers, and Redis gives it out of the box; any reactive mechanism works.

questions.q: How is the orchestrator kept from being a single point of failure?
questions.answer: Run it leader-follower with leader election: followers do work and one takes over in about 1-2 seconds if the leader fails.

questions.q: How does a public request reach a private load balancer?
questions.answer: Expose payments.google.com in public DNS pointing at the API gateway; the gateway forwards by path to lb.payments.google.com, resolved through private CoreDNS.

questions.q: What is the difference between a load balancer and a reverse proxy?
questions.answer: None really: load balancers are reverse proxies balancing across homogeneous servers; API gateways are powered-up proxies.

questions.q: Where does user authentication sit?
questions.answer: In the backend service's business logic, not the load balancer.

questions.q: Do orchestrator followers replicate state?
questions.answer: No, the orchestrator is stateless; all state is in the database.

questions.q: Is the Prometheus read side a bottleneck, and can it scale?
questions.answer: Reads are recent and light (one Prometheus can serve 50-100 LBs); scale with more query engines and replicated storage.

questions.q: Who initiates the heartbeat?
questions.answer: The orchestrator calls each backend's /health endpoint; the backend only answers.

questions.q: Must the health endpoint return 200, and should it check the database?
questions.answer: Accepted codes are configurable (200, 300...). Usually it just confirms the web server is up; checking the DB is your choice.

questions.q: Why don't backends push heartbeats to the orchestrator?
questions.answer: Backends don't know the orchestrator's IP and would need a sender thread; exposing /health is simpler for developers.

questions.q: Why is autoscaling separate from the orchestrator?
questions.answer: Customers configure scaling policies through an admin UI; split it out if the orchestrator gets too bulky, else the orchestrator does it.

questions.q: Who monitors the orchestrator?
questions.answer: Leader election, plus a minimal global monitor of the orchestrator masters with a standby: the base condition of the recursion.
